summary: Asks the community to share which socket numbers their standard service programs use. For example, loggers listen on socket 1. It suggests assigning socket 5 for the mail-box protocol of RFC 196 and asks whether some sockets should be reserved for future standard services.

plainLanguage.summary: Asking what door number each service uses so they will not clash. One door is for logging in; maybe another can be for mail.

questions: which sockets were used for standard services
how were well-known sockets assigned in 1971
what was socket 1 used for in 1971
subtitle: Jon Postel asks which standard programs listen on which socket numbers, and whether some should be reserved.

tldr.problem: Hosts run standard service programs on particular sockets, and there was no shared list or method for assigning those sockets.
tldr.mechanism: Postel asks sites to report which sockets their programs listen on, suggests socket 5 for a mail-box protocol, and asks whether a subset of socket numbers should be reserved for future standard protocols.
tldr.outcome: It is a request for information and opinions by phone or mail. The unit metadata shows it was updated by RFC 234.

today: RFC 204 is a request for comment; it was updated by RFC 234.

sections.title: Collecting Socket Usage
sections.content: Jon Postel wants to collect information on socket numbers used by standard service programs. His example is that Loggers (Telnet servers) listen on socket 1. He asks which sockets at each host are listened to by which programs.
sections.plainLanguage: He wants a list of which door number each helper program waits at.

sections.title: Proposals and Questions
sections.content:
Dick Watson recently suggested socket 5 for a mail-box protocol (RFC 196), and Postel asks whether anyone objects. He also asks for suggestions on a method for assigning sockets to standard programs, and whether a subset of socket numbers should be reserved for future standard protocols.

Replies are requested by phone or mail to the SPADE Group in the Computer Science Department.
sections.plainLanguage: He asks if door 5 can be for mail, how doors should be handed out, and whether some doors should be saved for later.

sections.title: What the RFC Is
sections.content: RFC 204 is a short note by Jon Postel, dated 5 August 71. It specifies nothing and reserves no sockets. It only gathers information and asks for opinions, and it is marked as related to RFC 196.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a question to the neighbors, not a rule. Nothing is decided yet.

references.text: Mail-box protocol, RFC 196, referenced as the protocol for socket 5.
